notes.body:
The one granted license (مأذون) is a **formally authorized representative** within the Ismaili da'wa hierarchy — "license" translates إذن, a word rooted in the idea of opening one's ear to someone and granting them access. The مأذون has been vetted, trusted, and appointed by someone of higher rank to act on behalf of the hierarchy in a defined space: a mosque, a city, or a region.

Authority flows downward through the ranks. At the summit sits the Imam; below him stand figures like the حجة and the داعي. It is typically the داعي who grants the license, effectively saying: "In this place, you represent us." The مأذون of Rajpur leads in Rajpur, and when two مأذون meet outside their own jurisdictions, the one whose mosque it is holds the stronger right.

Not all license-holders stand at the same level. An **unrestricted** مأذون holds considerably wider powers:

- He may appoint a substitute to complete the prayer if his own ablution breaks mid-prayer.
- He may lead a congregation even without having explicitly declared an intention to lead.
- When a figure of higher rank arrives, that person takes precedence — not as a challenge, but as the hierarchy expressing itself naturally.

The مأذون often prays among those who do not follow the way of the People of the House (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), and so تقية — protective concealment — becomes part of his daily practice. He may lower his voice when reciting:

بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

or omit the communal response:

رَبَّنَا لَكَ الْحَمْدُ
Our Lord, to You is all praise

when outsiders stand beside him. This is not weakness — it is **pastoral stewardship**, a recognition that preserving the community is itself a sacred act.

etymology: مأذون (one granted license): from the root أ-ذ-ن, meaning to open the ear and, by extension, to grant permission. مأذون is 'the one who has been permitted.' The same root gives إذن (permission) and أذان (the call to prayer): each is an act of opening access — one calls souls to worship, the other authorizes a person to serve.

تقية (protective concealment): from the root و-ق-ي, meaning to shield or ward off. The believer guards their faith by not exposing it to those who would harm them. The same root yields تقوى, Allah-consciousness: both centre on protection — تقوى guards the soul from sin; تقية guards the believer from danger.

داعي (summoner): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call, invite, or summon. The داعي is 'the one who calls,' inviting souls toward recognition of the Imam. The same root yields دعاء (supplication) and دعوة (the call or mission): calling upon Allah and calling others toward Him spring from the same impulse.

حجة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج, meaning to argue conclusively or establish proof. The حجة is the Imam's senior representative, whose authority is itself evidence of the Imam's presence. The same root gives حج, the pilgrimage: the pilgrim, like the حجة, travels toward an undeniable center.

notes.body:
The word نصيب, at its root, means a fixed allotment — a share formally set up and assigned to someone. When اَلْمُنْتَخَبَةُ says that "the nasib is set aside," it is referring to **the blind imam's own entitlement** to that act of leading. The three conditions اَلْمُنْتَخَبَةُ lays down form a coherent sequence: he may only lead when someone physically orients him; he cannot hold a permanent appointment as standing imam; and if he has led from the side, even that one-time leading does not stand.

"Leading from the side" describes an error almost unique to a blind imam. The imam stands at the head of the rows, squarely facing the قبلة and positioned ahead of everyone. A blind man who has not been properly set straight may drift laterally — ending up beside the first row rather than ahead of it, offset from the apex of the congregation. He might be reciting correctly and moving through every posture, yet standing to the left or right of the people rather than in front of them.

Think of it like a conductor who ends up standing among the musicians rather than facing them — the music may still play, but **the role itself has not been discharged**. His نصيب is cancelled. The blind imam's permission to lead is always conditional and narrow; this is the narrowest edge of that condition.

notes.quote: the nasib is set aside if he has led them from the side
etymology: نصيب (share, allotment): from the root ن-ص-ب, meaning to set up, erect, or fix firmly in place. A نصيب is a portion that has been stood up and formally appointed for a person — their fixed due. The فعيل pattern reinforces the sense of something established and stable. This is precisely why leading from the side forfeits it: what was fixed for the blind imam is undone by the irregularity of his position.

notes.body:
The standing of worshippers in prayer rows is not a matter of physical convenience alone — **it is a living map of spiritual rank**. In the Ismaili understanding, every act of outward worship carries an inner meaning (تأويل), and the arrangement of bodies in prayer mirrors the hierarchy of the sacred summons (دعوة).

The حجة occupies a unique position in this order. The word comes from the root ح-ج-ج, meaning to establish conclusive proof and to overcome in argument, and so the حجة is **the Imam's living proof** before the faithful. He is designated to stand in the Imam's place when the Imam is absent, carrying the Imam's authority downward through the ranks of the دعوة. This is not a ceremonial title — he is the Imam's active presence to those below him.

**Standing level with the imam** is therefore a privilege the text reserves exclusively for the حجة. When every row is full and an ordinary worshipper arrives, he prays alone to the side and never steps forward into the imam's rank — the prayer's outer form confirms that truth. But the حجة already belongs at that level of proximity — for him to stand apart would make the outer form lie about the inner reality.

Think of it like a court. **The chief deputy may share the bench** when no other seat remains, because his authority already belongs there; any other officer who did the same would be presuming beyond their rank. The prayer row works by the same logic: no one may claim a position above their standing in the spiritual order, even under necessity.

This coherence runs through all of Ismaili practice — **the outer form and the inner reality are always made to agree**. The visible (ظاهر) and the hidden (باطن) are not two separate worlds; they are the same truth seen from two directions. The prayer row is the دعوة made visible, each soul arranged by its proximity to truth, all prostrating together before Allah.

etymology: حجة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج, meaning to argue, to establish conclusive proof, and to overcome in disputation. The same root yields حج — pilgrimage — where both ideas converge in purposeful, directed movement toward a centre of truth. The حجة makes the Imam's reality undeniable to those who seek it.

دعوة (summons): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call, to summon, to invite toward. The same root gives دعاء (supplication) — in both cases a voice reaches across distance seeking response. The دعوة is the sacred call extended through the Imam's hierarchy, drawing souls toward the light of his authority.

إمام (leader): from the root أ-م-م, meaning to go before, to stand in front, to be a model others orient toward. Related to أمام (in front of), أم (mother — the one all return to), and أمة (community). The إمام is the one through whom direction is found; to follow him is to be oriented toward truth.

تأويل (inner meaning): from the root أ-و-ل, meaning to return to the first principle, to trace a thing back to its source. The تأويل of an act is not interpretation in the ordinary sense — it is the restoration of its original depth. The root ties meaning-making to the idea of return.

ظاهر (outward): from the root ظ-ه-ر, meaning to appear, to be manifest, to rise to the surface. The same root gives ظهر (back — the visible side of the body) and ظهور (emergence). In Ismaili thought, the ظاهر is the surface of a truth whose depth the باطن holds.

باطن (hidden): from the root ب-ط-ن, meaning to be concealed within, to lie in the interior. The same root gives بطن (belly — the interior of the body). What is باطن lies inside, invisible to the surface glance. Every outward form carries a باطن that gives it its real and lasting meaning.
